 ## Search results
BERT4Rec’s objective mismatch is explicitly acknowledged in the [original paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.06690): reconstructing interior masked items can use future context, whereas appended-MASK prediction has only history. [Recency Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643) argues that item masking is weakly related to next-item prediction and can require substantially more training. These findings motivate terminal supervision, but do not establish that reconstruction necessarily harms transfer. A recent related approach, [Masked History Learning (2025; revised 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23649), combines next-item learning with auxiliary history reconstruction in generative recommendation; its results do not directly establish effectiveness for BERT4Rec.

Practical hypothesis for one shared BERT4Rec: sample a training cutoff t, input only [x₁,…,xₜ₋₁,MASK], and predict xₜ from the terminal mask. Exclude the target occurrence and all later positions from this input. Use a separate corrupted-history forward pass through the same network for reconstruction. Optimize L = mean(terminal cross-entropy) + λ·mean(reconstruction cross-entropy), averaging each loss over its own valid targets before weighting. This is a proposed experiment, not a verified recipe from the retrieved papers. Preserve reserved MASK tokens, appended-mask inference, and final-nonpadding-position readout under left padding.

Measure gradients of each loss on shared parameters: cosine similarity, fraction of batches with negative cosine, and gradient norm ratio. [PCGrad](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.06782) identifies negative gradient dot products as conflict and projects conflicting components away. It supplies a diagnostic and possible intervention, not evidence that these particular BERT4Rec objectives conflict. Compare terminal-only training against the joint objective using fixed-budget macro validation HR@10.

---

[TemProxRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.09784) is the closest match: BERT-style masked-item training with attention encoding absolute timestamps/positions and relative time/position differences. Its ablations support temporal attention: on Amazon Beauty, NDCG@10 falls from 0.365 to 0.352 without relative attention and to 0.347 with canonical attention; removing its auxiliary temporal contrastive loss yields 0.357. However, these ablations remove time and position components together, so they do not isolate temporal benefit against an otherwise identical position-only model. Datasets and sampled evaluation also differ from the pinned RecHarness task; reported gains are hypotheses, not transferable estimates.

[TLSTSRec (online 2024; volume 2025)](https://doi.org/10.3233/IDA-240051) models duration and temporal spectrum with trainable timestamp matrices and adaptive long/short-term fusion. A [2026 BERT4Rec session-enhancement paper](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01554-z) combines content attention with continuous time decay and gated long/short representations, but its branch and deployment changes prevent clean attribution to relative-time attention. Practical hypothesis: retain one jointly trained BERT4Rec per category and add learned, head-specific relative-time biases alongside position embeddings. Compare against the identical position-only backbone under fixed training and validation. Use observed historical timestamps only; assign the appended mask a history-derived temporal reference rather than the unknown target timestamp. Preserve masked-target training and final-nonpadding readout. Interpret recent intent and persistent affinity as latent model behavior, not observed simulator traits.

---

Recent evidence supports text-enhanced recommendation, but does not establish that a scratch-trained ID+text BERT4Rec will improve this benchmark. [JEPA4Rec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.10512v3) jointly learns textual item representations and sequential preferences, but uses pretrained language knowledge and a different training framework. [Dual-View Whitening (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v38i8.28786) finds benefits from reducing pretrained text-embedding anisotropy, while warning that full whitening can damage semantic structure. These results motivate an experiment with a small, randomly initialized title/description encoder jointly integrated into one BERT4Rec network; they do not validate that exact design or justify importing pretrained weights.

Hard negatives require caution: [Enhanced BPR (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) identifies potential positives mislabeled as negatives as a source of misleading gradients. [Negative-sampling experiments (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) also show dataset-dependent accuracy and popularity tradeoffs. A reasonable hypothesis is gradual, mixed random/semi-hard sampling, excluding observed training positives, rather than hardest-only mining.
